passage: So, Salma, remember the week I sulked about the eight o'clock rule? Here is what I did after. I was so sure Mum and Dad thought I couldn't be trusted that I had stopped asking. Then I thought: if I'm wrong about their reason, all my arguing is aimed at the wrong thing. So at dinner I asked, "What exactly worries you about late evenings?" Dad put down his spoon. He said it wasn't about me. It was the road home: the stretch by the flyover has no lights, and the last bus is unreliable. Mum said she just wanted to know I'd arrived. I sat there feeling a bit silly. It was never about trust. So I said, "What if I'm picked up from Salma's by ten?" and the whole conversation changed. I'm Hemant, and it took one question.

qa.q: What did Hemant ask at dinner?
qa.a: Hemant asked, 'What exactly worries you about late evenings?'

qa.q: How did Hemant feel on learning the parents' real reason?
qa.a: Hemant felt a little silly and relieved, since the worry was about the dark road home and not about trust.

qa.q: What could Hemant add to the pick-up idea to reassure the parents, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could send a message on arriving and set the exact pick-up time, because those steps answer the worry about the road home.

qa.q: How might Hemant's parents see the question at dinner?
qa.a: They probably feel heard and respected, since Hemant asked about their worry and did not simply argue.

grounding: The teenager asks why the parents refuse late evenings and learns the concern is safety and late-night travel, not distrust, which allows a plan that addresses those concerns.

passage: I'm Hrithik, Suraj's cousin, and I was staying with them the week of the big argument. Suraj wanted to go to a friend's birthday dinner that finished at eleven, and his parents kept saying no. On Tuesday he stopped arguing and asked, "Can you just tell me why? Is it that you don't trust me?" Mausi put down her spoon. "We trust you. It's the road. The last bus is at ten, and autos on that route at night aren't safe. Last year a boy from your school was hurt." Mausa nodded. "It's the travel, not you." I watched Suraj's shoulders drop. Then he said, "What if Papa picks me up at ten-thirty from the restaurant door?" They looked at each other. "That we can do," Mausa said.

qa.q: What did Suraj's shoulders dropping suggest?
qa.a: It suggested he felt relieved to hear the worry was about the road, not distrust.

qa.q: Why did asking why change the conversation?
qa.a: It revealed the real worry, late-night travel, so Suraj could offer a plan that answered it directly.

qa.q: How did Mausi and Mausa see the question?
qa.a: They seemed glad to explain that they trusted Suraj and were worried only about the road, and quickly agreed to the pick-up.

grounding: An observer sees a teenager ask why late evenings are refused, learn the worry is late-night travel, and propose a pick-up plan.

passage:
Monday. Karthik's parents say no to Rafiq's Friday movie night, which ends at eleven. Karthik slams his door and texts Rafiq: "They think I'm a baby."
Wednesday. At dinner, calmer, he asks Appa, "Is it that you don't trust me, or something else?" Appa thinks. "It's the flyover at night. There have been accidents, and you'd be on the back of Rafiq's brother's bike." Amma adds, "And we can't reach you when your phone dies." Karthik hadn't thought about either.
Friday. Karthik takes a charged power bank, goes to Rafiq's by auto at six, and Appa picks him up by car at 10:45. At 10:50, from the back seat, he messages Rafiq: "Best movie night. Same deal next month?"

qa.q: Whose bike would Karthik have been on?
How did Karthik feel on Monday?
qa.a: He felt angry and hurt, slamming his door, believing his parents thought he was a baby.

qa.q: What made Friday's plan work for everyone?
qa.a: It answered each worry directly: no bike on the flyover, a charged power bank so he could be reached, and Appa picking him up.

qa.q: How might Appa feel picking Karthik up at 10:45?
qa.a: Appa probably feels relieved and more trusting, since the plan took his worries seriously.

grounding: Shows over a week a teenager asking why his parents refuse, learning the worries are the night road and reachability, and planning around them.
